title: Sysctl Assignment Invocation Detection (Linux)
exclusions: Detects successful `execve` launches of the locally resolved procps `sysctl` executable when an `EXECVE` argument has `parameter=value` form. It does not prove that the utility successfully wrote the value, detect `sysctl --system` or `sysctl -p`, detect direct writes such as `echo 1 > /proc/sys/...`, watch persistent files under `/etc/sysctl.d`, or cover changes made before Linux Audit and the Splunk input were healthy. It deliberately does not claim that a wildcard or recursive Audit watch on the procfs `/proc/sys` tree is portable.
evidence: When deployed, retain the `linux_sysctl_assignment_invocation` saved-search definition and dispatch history, the matching raw `SYSCALL` and `EXECVE` records identified by `host` and `msg`, the alert result containing `parameter`, `requested_value`, `audit_exe`, and `actor_auid`, and a contemporaneous `auditctl -l` export showing the host-specific `sysctl_write` rule. These artifacts show observed write intent; they are not proof that the requested kernel value took effect.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Index two synthetic `sourcetype=auditd` records on host `sysctl-test` with the same `msg=audit(1760000000.100:422)`: a `type=SYSCALL` record containing `success=yes`, `exe=/usr/sbin/sysctl`, `auid=1001`, and `key=sysctl_write`, plus a `type=EXECVE` record containing `a0=sysctl`, `a1=-w`, and `a2=net.ipv4.ip_forward=1`. Over a time range containing both records, the search must return exactly one row with `parameter=net.ipv4.ip_forward`, `requested_value=1`, and `actor_auid=1001`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Index a matched synthetic pair on host `sysctl-test` with `msg=audit(1760000001.100:423)`, `key=sysctl_write`, and `success=yes`, but set the `EXECVE` arguments to `a0=sysctl`, `a1=-n`, and `a2=net.ipv4.ip_forward` with no equals sign. Also index an assignment pair with `success=no`. The search must return no row for either serial because a read-only invocation has no assignment and a failed `execve` did not launch the utility.

dataSources: `index=os sourcetype=auditd` events from the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) `rlog.sh` scripted input, which translates Linux Audit data with `ausearch`. The SPL requires `host`, `type`, `msg`, `key`, `success`, `exe`, `auid`, and `a0` through `a9`; the `os` index is a local deployment choice, while `auditd` and `rlog.sh` are add-on-defined.
app: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) 10.3.1 or another release explicitly compatible with the local Splunk platform. Linux `auditd`, `auditctl`, `augenrules`, and procps `sysctl` are host prerequisites, not Splunk apps.
spl:
index=os sourcetype=auditd [ search index=os sourcetype=auditd type=SYSCALL key=sysctl_write
| fields host msg
| dedup host msg
| append [ | makeresults
| eval host="__no_sysctl_write__", msg="__no_sysctl_write__"
| fields host msg ]
| format ]
| where type="SYSCALL" OR type="EXECVE"
| eval audit_args=if(type="EXECVE",mvappend(a0,a1,a2,a3,a4,a5,a6,a7,a8,a9),null())
| stats earliest(_time) as _time values(type) as record_types values(success) as audit_success values(exe) as audit_exe values(auid) as actor_auid values(audit_args) as audit_args by host msg
| eval assignment=mvfilter(match(audit_args,"^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+="))
| where mvfind(record_types,"^SYSCALL$")>=0 AND mvfind(record_types,"^EXECVE$")>=0 AND mvfind(audit_success,"^(yes|1)$")>=0 AND mvcount(assignment)>0
| eval assignment=mvindex(assignment,0), parameter=replace(assignment,"=.*$",""), requested_value=replace(assignment,"^[^=]+=","")
| eval audit_exe=mvindex(audit_exe,0), actor_auid=mvindex(actor_auid,0)
| table _time host parameter requested_value audit_exe actor_auid msg
description: Detects Linux Audit events for a successful launch of the locally resolved procps `sysctl` executable when its linked `EXECVE` record includes a `parameter=value` argument. Each result represents one host and Linux Audit event identifier (`msg`) within the scheduled window; it reports an attempted runtime assignment, not confirmation that the kernel accepted or retained the value.
value: Rapid attribution of kernel-tuning attempts helps platform teams reduce the time spent explaining routing, memory, and hardening drift after an outage or security change. Showing the login audit identity, executable, requested parameter, and requested value gives responders a precise starting point for change-ticket correlation and host verification without overstating the event as a completed change.
implementation: Resolve the procps `sysctl` executable separately on each Linux image, add a narrow architecture-correct Linux Audit `execve` rule for that absolute executable with key `sysctl_write`, and prove that the rule emits linked `SYSCALL` and `EXECVE` records before rollout. Enable the add-on's `rlog.sh` input as `sourcetype=auditd`, schedule a five-minute search with a six-minute lookback, and alert on every returned event after applying exact, expiring change-window exceptions.
visualization: Use a latest-first table with `_time`, `host`, `parameter`, `requested_value`, `audit_exe`, and `actor_auid`; add a 24-hour timechart of invocation count by parameter and a drilldown to all records sharing `host` and `msg`. Label every panel "assignment invocation" rather than "value changed".

knownFalsePositives:
1. **OpenSCAP remediation script** — Generated remediation can invoke `sysctl -w` for a named hardening parameter. Correlate `_time`, `host`, `parameter`, and `actor_auid` with the OpenSCAP job report; suppress only the exact parameters in that job's approved window.

2. **Ansible `command` or `shell` task** — A playbook may explicitly run `/usr/sbin/sysctl -w parameter=value`. Match the host and minute to the Ansible Automation Platform job ID and inventory; do not suppress the Ansible service account outside that job's start and end times.

3. **systemd one-shot tuning unit** — A locally authored unit with `ExecStart=...sysctl -w...` can run during boot or service recovery. Confirm the unit name and invocation in the systemd journal, then allow-list only its executable, host class, parameter set, and boot-relative window.

4. **Kubernetes node-bootstrap command** — A cluster bootstrap script can call procps `sysctl -w` before kubelet starts. Distinguish it with the node-pool rollout record and bootstrap service identity; suppress the exact node image version and provisioning interval rather than all activity by root.

5. **Approved operator troubleshooting** — A platform engineer may temporarily change `net.ipv4.ip_forward`, `vm.swappiness`, or another parameter while diagnosing an incident. Require a live incident or change ticket, compare `actor_auid` with the assigned responder, verify the current value on the host, and expire the exception when the test ends.

**Suppression mechanism:** apply `linux_sysctl_write_exceptions.csv` after the core search, keyed by exact `host`, `parameter`, `audit_exe`, and `actor_auid`, with `valid_from`, `valid_until`, `change_ticket`, and `owner`. Reject wildcard parameters and rows without an expiry; preserve suppressed events for review.
mitreAttack: N/A (assignment monitoring does not establish attacker intent or an ATT&CK technique)
reviewer: documentation review against Splunk, Linux Audit, Linux kernel, and procps primary sources
detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and semantic boundary

Assign a Linux platform owner and a Splunk content owner. Install a release of the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) that its compatibility matrix supports for the local Splunk Enterprise or Splunk Cloud deployment; this review used the 10.3.1 documentation. Put the add-on on the Universal Forwarder for `rlog.sh` and on the search tier for its knowledge objects. Grant the search role access to the selected operating-system index. The catalogue calls that index `os`; it is a deployment choice, not a vendor default.

The signal is intentionally narrower than the old title implied. Linux Audit `path` and `dir` filters are inode/tree watches, wildcards are not supported, and the `perm=w` filter selects operations from requested open flags; it does not prove that bytes were written or that a sysctl value changed. Procfs support for a `/proc/sys` watch must not be assumed across kernels. This implementation therefore audits execution of the procps `sysctl` utility and looks for its documented `variable=value` argument form. A successful `execve` means that the utility started, not that its later write succeeded. Direct `/proc/sys` redirection, `sysctl --system`, and alternate writers remain outside scope.

## 1. Configure and prove the Linux Audit rule

On each supported image, resolve the executable with `command -v sysctl`, canonicalize it with `readlink -f`, and confirm its ABI with `file`. Do not copy `/sbin/sysctl` or `/usr/sbin/sysctl` from this document into every host policy. The `auditctl` `exe` field requires an absolute path and can occur only once per rule. Build one exit-filter rule for the actual native ABI, place `arch=b64` or `arch=b32` before `-S execve`, filter `exe` on the resolved path, and assign the key `sysctl_write`. A representative x86-64 host whose resolved executable really is `/usr/sbin/sysctl` would use `-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -F exe=/usr/sbin/sysctl -F key=sysctl_write`; that path is an example, not a portable default.

Store the reviewed rule in a `.rules` file under `/etc/audit/rules.d/`. Run `augenrules --check`, then load it through the distribution's approved audit workflow. Confirm the effective rule with `auditctl -l`. If audit is immutable (`auditctl -s` reports enabled value 2), schedule the rule for the next controlled reboot instead of weakening audit. If `auditctl` rejects the executable or ABI, stop and correct the host policy; do not compensate by removing the `exe` filter and auditing every `execve`.

In an isolated test VM, capture the original value of an approved test parameter, invoke the resolved utility with a concrete assignment, immediately restore the original, and inspect `ausearch -k sysctl_write -i`. The event must contain linked `SYSCALL` and `EXECVE` records with the same audit timestamp and serial. Verify `success=yes`, the expected `exe`, a meaningful login `auid`, and an argument containing `=`. This is a collection qualification step. It must be repeated for each kernel/image family and recorded; documentation review alone does not establish runtime support.

## 2. Collect and verify `auditd` events

Enable the add-on's existing `rlog.sh` scripted input in `Splunk_TA_nix/local/inputs.conf`; do not edit the add-on's `default` directory. The add-on documents `rlog.sh` as reading Linux Auditing System information from `/var/log/audit/audit.log`, translating it with `ausearch`, and assigning `sourcetype=auditd`. If the distribution does not write that file or the script cannot execute `ausearch`, this collection path is not qualified until the platform owner selects a supported alternative.

Run the Universal Forwarder without unnecessary root privilege. Give its service identity only the file access and command capability required by the supported add-on procedure, including access after audit-log rotation. Use `splunk btool inputs list --debug` to verify the winning `rlog.sh` stanza, interval, sourcetype, and `index=os` routing. Then search `index=os sourcetype=auditd key=sysctl_write` and compare two `msg` identifiers with `ausearch -k sysctl_write -i` on the same host.

Do not schedule the alert until `type`, `msg`, `key`, `success`, `exe`, `auid`, and the `EXECVE` argument fields are present. One Linux Audit event consists of several records sharing a timestamp and serial; the search uses `host` plus `msg` to reunite them. The add-on documents no CIM model for `sourcetype=auditd`, so no `tstats` substitute is claimed. Monitor `auditctl -s` for a rising `lost` count and the Universal Forwarder internal logs for scripted-input failures; either condition creates a coverage gap.

## 3. Create the search and alert

Save the SPL as `linux_sysctl_assignment_invocation`. Run it every five minutes over the previous six minutes to tolerate normal forwarding delay. The inner search selects only `SYSCALL` records carrying `key=sysctl_write` and formats their `host`/`msg` pairs as a constraint for the outer search. It appends an impossible sentinel pair so an empty subsearch cannot broaden the outer search to every `auditd` event. This avoids grouping the fleet's complete `execve` stream. The outer search retrieves the linked `SYSCALL` and `EXECVE` records, collects the first ten argument fields, and groups them by host and audit event identifier.

The `assignment` expression retains arguments matching `parameter=value`. Requiring both record types, a successful `execve`, and at least one assignment removes read-only commands such as `sysctl -n net.ipv4.ip_forward`. The result is one row per invocation. There is no count threshold: one unreviewed assignment is operationally relevant. The six-minute lookback is a completeness allowance, not a risk threshold. Trigger when result count is greater than zero and throttle duplicate notifications by `host` plus `msg` for 15 minutes.

The SPL intentionally examines `a0` through `a9`. If local automation supplies an assignment later than the tenth argument, extend the field list only after indexing a representative event and adding a control test. If the inner subsearch approaches Splunk's subsearch-result limit, that indicates an unexpectedly high volume of `sysctl_write` executions; shorten the interval or route this key to a dedicated audit index rather than broadening the filter.

Apply `linux_sysctl_write_exceptions.csv` only after the core logic passes. Match exact `host`, `parameter`, `audit_exe`, and `actor_auid`, parse `valid_from` and `valid_until`, and retain rows outside the approved interval. Require a change ticket and owner. Never exclude all root activity: `auid` is intended to preserve the login identity even when effective UID is zero, while an unset `auid` is itself a triage condition.

## 4. Validate the saved search

Run the positive and negative synthetic scenarios in `controlTest` and preserve the search-job inspector output. The positive pair must produce exactly one row; the read-only and `success=no` pairs must produce none. Add a second positive pair with a different `msg` serial to prove that aggregation does not merge independent invocations.

On the isolated host, compare the Splunk result with `ausearch -k sysctl_write -i --start recent`. Confirm the same host, audit serial, executable, login audit ID, and assignment argument. Then query 24 hours with `index=os sourcetype=auditd | timechart span=5m count by type` and investigate gaps longer than two `rlog.sh` intervals. Separately compare the requested value with a direct read of the parameter on the host. A mismatch is possible and must be shown as a failed or superseded assignment, not hidden by changing the alert label to "changed".

Test rule health after an audit package update, a forwarder upgrade, log rotation, and a host reboot. Confirm that the persistent rule reloads, `rlog.sh` resumes without rereading an excessive backlog, and `auditctl -s` reports no new lost events. These are documented acceptance checks; this catalogue record does not claim they were executed in a customer environment.

## 5. Operationalize and troubleshoot

Build a dashboard with a latest-first invocation table, a 24-hour count by parameter, and a host drilldown that retrieves every record sharing the selected `msg`. Restrict requested values because some organizations place sensitive strings in kernel parameters. Route network parameters to the network-platform owner, virtual-memory parameters to Linux SRE, and hardening parameters to the security-engineering queue. The runbook must verify the current value, compare the event with change automation and a ticket, determine whether the assignment persisted, and restore only through the approved configuration source.

No `sysctl_write` events after a known test usually means the rule uses the wrong executable path or ABI, was not loaded, or audit is immutable; compare `readlink -f`, `file`, `auditctl -l`, and `auditctl -s`. A `SYSCALL` without `EXECVE` fields indicates incomplete ingestion or a time-range boundary; inspect the same `msg` with `ausearch` and widen the lookback. Null `key`, `success`, or `aN` fields points to the wrong sourcetype or missing search-tier knowledge objects; confirm `sourcetype=auditd` and the add-on deployment. Duplicate alerts come from overlapping windows; preserve `msg` and throttle on `host,msg`. An unset `auid` can arise from a non-login service context; route it for service-owner attribution instead of replacing it with `uid`. A rising audit `lost` count means kernel backlog pressure and invalidates completeness until the audit owner tunes capacity. A silent `rlog.sh` input commonly reflects permission, `ausearch`, rotation, or script-state problems; use `btool` and forwarder internal logs before changing the SPL. Finally, a result with the old value still present is not a false parser result: it demonstrates why this UC records assignment intent and requires host-side outcome verification.
grandmaExplanation: We flag when a person or automated job starts the standard Linux command with instructions to change a live kernel setting. The team can then check whether the attempt was approved and whether the setting actually took effect.
